analysis.one_liner: Extends federal oversight to nonbank companies that own FDIC-insured industrial banks.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without any hearing or vote after being introduced in the final month of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Industrial banks, or ILCs, are state-chartered lenders that can take FDIC-insured deposits while being owned by regular companies — fintechs, payment processors, retailers — whose parent companies escape supervision by the Federal Reserve, a gap known as the shadow banking loophole. This bill would close it: parent companies of ILCs would face the same FDIC reporting and examination powers that apply to regular bank holding companies, new deposit insurance approvals would be harder to get, and pending applications not approved by September 2023 would be denied. It was introduced on December 6, 2022 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors and taxpayers, who ultimately back the FDIC deposit insurance fund, gain because companies that take insured deposits would no longer operate their parent businesses outside federal examination. Consumers who use fintech lending and payment products gain a backstop against the failure of a lightly supervised parent. Traditional, fully regulated banks gain a more level playing field against nonbank competitors holding insured deposits.

how_it_helps.text: The FDIC would gain the same authority over parent companies of industrial loan companies to require reports and conduct examinations that the Federal Reserve has over bank holding companies.

Pending deposit insurance applications from industrial banks would require a 90-day public comment period, a public hearing, and approval by a two-thirds vote of the FDIC board, and any application not approved by September 23, 2023 would be deemed denied.

Transfers of control of an industrial bank would generally be disapproved unless the buyer is itself subject to consolidated Federal Reserve supervision, keeping the charter from moving to unsupervised owners.

analysis.who_pays: Nonfinancial companies that own, or want to own, FDIC-insured industrial banks — fintech lenders, payment companies, and retailers — would bear the cost of full parent-company supervision, and firms with applications pending since before September 2021 would likely see those applications denied. Some consumers could see less fintech competition in lending and payments if the charter becomes much harder to obtain.

drawbacks.text: The bill draws a sharp line at September 23, 2021: industrial banks with deposit insurance approved on or before that date keep their charter and their exemption from the Bank Holding Company Act, while anyone after faces full treatment — an arbitrary cutoff that entrenches incumbents and could equally have been drawn to exclude them.

A good-faith objection is that the ILC charter exists to let nonbank companies offer lending and payment services, sometimes to consumers underserved by traditional banks, and making the charter far harder to obtain could reduce that competition without meaningfully reducing risk, since the FDIC already insures and can supervise the insured banks themselves.
Deeming pending applications denied on a fixed date, rather than reviewing each on its merits, could terminate applicants by deadline rather than by evaluation of their safety.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core goal — making sure companies that hold FDIC-insured deposits answer to a federal supervisor — addresses a real gap in the financial regulatory system, and the public interest in oversight of insured deposits is genuine. But the bill's design is blunt: the September 2021 cutoff locks in every incumbent ILC while cutting off future entrants, which weakens competition even as it tightens oversight. A better-designed version might have applied the same supervision rules to everyone rather than splitting the industry by date.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced in December 2022 and sat there until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, never receiving a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the Close the Shadow Banking Loophole Act in the Senate on December 6, 2022, joined by Senators Casey and Van Hollen.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have subjected parent companies of industrial loan companies to FDIC reporting and examination authority comparable to what the Federal Reserve applies to bank holding companies, a supervisory gap the CRS summary describes as leaving those parents unsupervised by the Federal Reserve.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nonfinancial companies that hold or seek industrial bank charters — fintech lenders, payment processors, and retailers — are better off, because the loophole that lets their parent companies operate outside Federal Reserve-style supervision stays open. Traditional banks that wanted the competitive gap closed are worse off.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), bill sponsor and Chair of the Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bring parent companies of industrial banks under federal supervision.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded support was three Democratic senators, and no one is recorded as having opposed it — it simply ran out of Congress.

industries.industry: Nonfinancial parent companies of industrial banks (fintech lenders, payment processors, retailers)
industries.note: The bill grandfathers every ILC with FDIC deposit insurance approved on or before September 23, 2021, keeping those companies' charter privileges intact, while adding tailored FDIC examination authority over their parents. Incumbents keep the loophole that lets them take insured deposits without full parent-company supervision; the public's interest in oversight of insured deposits runs against that arrangement.

industries.industry: Fintech and nonbank companies seeking new ILC charters
industries.note: Pending applications would need a two-thirds FDIC board vote and would be deemed denied if not approved by September 2023, and future approvals would come with the exemption from bank holding company rules removed. Consumers could lose some lower-cost fintech credit and payment options, but would gain regulated, supervised providers.

industries.industry: Traditional banks and regulated bank holding companies
industries.note: Full regulation of ILC parents removes competition from charters that take insured deposits without equivalent oversight of their owners, leveling the field that existing banks already operate under.
